title: Advance Screening of The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping
description: A free "End the Stigma" festival will begin at 7:30 p.m. and feature mental health learning stations, activities, giveaways, information about campus programs and snacks. The event will take place at the IMU Whittenberger Auditorium.  The event is sponsored by University Bring Change to Mind (UBC2M), a student-centered college program associated with Bring Change to Mind, the nonprofit founded by Glenn Close and her family. Through student-led efforts, UBC2M encourages connection and open conversations about mental health while working to reduce stigma surrounding mental illness. The program is housed in IU's Irsay Institute, which conducts research on mental health, addiction and other health care issues.  From acclaimed director Francis Lawrence, THE HUNGER GAMES: SUNRISE ON THE REAPING follows sixteen-year-old Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada) from District 12, beginning on the morning of the reaping for the 50th Annual Hunger Games, also known as the Second Quarter Quell, the biggest Games yet with twice as many tributes.  Set in the world of Panem 24 years before the events of The Hunger Games, the story follows Haymitch into the arena, where he forms an unlikely alliance with fellow tribute Maysilee Donner (Mckenna Grace) and joins a coalition determined to challenge the Capitol's control under President Snow (Ralph Fiennes). As the competition unfolds, Haymitch risks everything to take down the Games from within the arena, setting in motion the rebellion that will change Panem forever.  Tickets are free, however, there will be opportunities to donate if desired. Proceeds will support student mental health events and opportunities on campus.

title: Palestine 36 w/ filmmaker | Arthouse Now
description: In 1936, as the British Empire tightens its grip on Palestine, Yusuf is caught between his village home and his work in Jerusalem. Amidst an anti-colonial revolt and a workers uprising, all sides converge in a decisive moment for the entire region. Weaving together multiple plotlines, empathies, and frames of reference, Annemarie Jacir deftly balances intimate human stories—portrayed by a stellar ensemble cast—with sweeping political history, using rare archival footage to ground the narrative in historical reality. [119 min; drama; Arabic with English subtitles and English]A prerecorded conversation with filmmaker Annemarie Jacir, unique to IU Cinema, will screen after the film. Jacir has written, directed, and produced over 16 films. Her films have premiered in Cannes, Berlin, Venice, Locarno, Rotterdam, and Toronto. Her second work to debut in Cannes, Salt of This Sea, went on to win the FIPRESCI Critics Award, and 14 other international awards including Best Film in Milan. With a commitment to mentoring, training, and hiring locally, Jacir also teaches, actively promoting independent cinema in the region. Founder of Philistine Films, she collaborates regularly as an editor, screenwriter, and producer with fellow filmmakers.

title: Pei-San Chiu, flute; Jessica Warren, oboe; Melivia Raharjo, piano; Hsuan Chang Kitano, harpsichord
description: Enjoy this performance from almost anywhere in the world viaLIVE@jacobs!Repertoire  Quantz: Trio Sonata in C Minor, QV 2:Anh. 5Ginastera: Duo, Op. 13 (1945)Dring : Trio (1968)Still: Miniatures (1948)Gaubert: Tarentelle (1903)About the ArtistPei-San Chiu is an internationally acclaimed Taiwanese flutist and educator. She debuted at Carnegie Hall in 2012 as first-prize winner of the Alexander & Buono International Flute Competition and has performed across the United States, Brazil, Japan, South Korea, Hong Kong, China, and Singapore in solo, chamber, and orchestral settings. From 2013 to 2016, she served as principal flute of the Lexington Philharmonic, garnering praise for her "character and vitality" (Lexington Herald-Leader), and has performed as guest principal with the National Symphony Orchestra in Taiwan, Guangzhou Symphony, and Shenzhen Symphony. A passionate advocate for contemporary music, she has commissioned and premiered works by Bin Li, Tsung-Jen Hsieh, Mei-Chun Chen, Zhou Tian, and Yu-Chun Hu. Her solo album Air, featuring works by female composers, was nominated for Best Art Music Album at the 2025 Golden Melody Awards in Taiwan. She also performs with the Formosa Trio, Aureus Duo, and Trio 2:1, releasing albums including First Impression, Anniversary, and The Sound of Flowers. Chiu is associate professor of flute at Tunghai University, where she received the 2020 Teaching Excellence Award, and adjunct associate professor of flute at the Indiana University Jacobs School of Music. She earned Master of Music and Doctor of Music degrees from the Jacobs School. Chiu continues to inspire audiences and students alike through her innovative artistry and dedication to advancing the flute repertoire and pedagogy.Hsuan Chang Kitano is adjunct lecturer in music in historical performance (fortepiano and harpsichord) at the Indiana University Jacobs School of Music, where she has been on faculty since 2013. Her performance and recording engagements on fortepiano, harpsichord, basso continuo, and piano have taken her to prominent venues in Taiwan, Singapore, Malaysia, Germany, Italy, and the United States. A prizewinning keyboard soloist, she has been the winner of the Indianapolis Baroque Orchestra/Early Music Institute Concerto Competition (harpsichord) and the Early Music Institute Concerto Competition (fortepiano). Her playing on harpsichord and fortepiano has been praised for its "elegance with admirable clarity" (The Herald-Times). Kitano is an active scholar in the field of eighteenth-century keyboard music. Her research on improvisation in keyboard music of the Classical Era was influenced by Robert Levin while she worked as a visiting scholar at Harvard University. Her historical keyboard performances have been informed by master classes of Skip Sempé, Pierre Hantai, Christopher Rousset, Trevor Pinnock, and Malcolm Bilson. Kitano's current research focuses on intercultural musical improvisation. Building on her knowledge of historical performance practice of Baroque thorough bass and eighteenth-century improvisation on cadenza and Eingänge, she has conducted collaborative projects with traditional music of India, Taiwan, and China. She also works with museums on historical keyboard instrument restoration in addition to a project regarding a different tuning system on her recording of the Bach Goldberg Variations at Zuckermann Harpsichords International. Kitano earned D.M. and M.M. degrees from the Jacobs School.Melivia Raharjo is lecturer in music in collaborative piano at the Indiana University Jacobs School of Music. Born in Indonesia, she is an avid collaborative pianist and has appeared in chamber performances with such renowned artists as the Takcs Quartet, Roger Vignoles, Jaime Laredo, Olga Dubossarskaya Kaler, Mark Kosower, and Richard Weiss. One of the official pianists of the 11th International Violin Competition of Indianapolis in 2022, she was awarded special prizes for best performances of the Mozart and Beethoven sonatas with gold medalist Sirena Huang. She also has been playing for the cello master class program in Hidden Valley Music Seminar since 2022. Raharjo is a Music Academy of the West alumna and won the Duo Competition with violist Keoni Bolding in 2021. As part of the prize package, they performed a recital in Santa Barbara for which they created a program including special lighting effects to enhance its theme of night, from dusk through dawn. The recital also included the world premiere of Conrad Tao's "Churn." Previously, she worked as a staff pianist at the Cleveland Institute of Music, where she studied with Anita Pontremoli for her master's degree and artist diploma in collaborative piano. Raharjo discovered her passion in collaborating with other musicians while pursuing a bachelor's degree at Yong Siew Toh Conservatory of Music in Singapore, studying with Albert Tiu. Performing with other musicians who are passionate about music brings so much joy to her life she hopes that their performances inspire others to play more chamber music in the future.Jessica Warren is adjunct associate professor of music in oboe at the Indiana University Jacobs School of Music. She performs regularly with leading ensembles including the National Symphony Orchestra, Kennedy Center Opera House Orchestra, Wintergreen Festival Orchestra, and Berkshire Bach Society. She recently served as guest principal oboe with the United States Air Force Band during its spring 2024 multistate tour. A Jacobs School alumna and two-time fellow at the Tanglewood Music Center, Warren brings significant teaching experience from positions at George Washington University, the Interlochen Center for the Arts, and the New England Conservatory. Warren specializes in oboe reedmaking education and oboe gouging machine training. Her dissertation, "Significant Learning as Reedmaking Pedagogy," evaluated and reimagined collegiate reedmaking curricula. She regularly presents lectures and master classes in the area of mindfulness in reedmaking and practicing. Warren earned a Doctor of Musical Arts degree from Boston University, studying under John Ferrillo. She earned a Performer Diploma and a Master of Music degree under Linda Strommen at Jacobs and a bachelor's degree under Robert Sorton at The Ohio State University.

title: Daniel Luis Martinez: The Blueprint | Exhibition
location: The Contemporary Art Museum of Indianapolis
description: Opening reception: Friday, October 2, 2026, 6–10pm  Exhibition on view: October 2–December 18, 2026  For this exhibition, the blueprint is used as both a representational and conceptual departure point. Daniel Luis Martinez uses cyanotype printmaking and mixed-media drawing techniques as a generative process to imagine a speculative home on the CAMi campus. The hybrid drawings and prints featured in the exhibition explore the tactile middle-ground of the blueprint as a creative endeavor.  The series employs orthographic conventions typical of architectural drawing sets, though not as precise instructions for building. Rather, a layered and loose approach expresses ideas of home as an architectonic language.  Daniel Luis Martinez is a registered architect, educator, and co-founder of the multi-disciplinary design studio LAA Office, which explores the intersection of landscape, art, and architecture. His research and creative work investigate the potential of public art to generate alternative forms of placemaking. Martinez is Associate Professor and Director of the IU Eskenazi School's J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program (https://architecture.indiana.edu/index.html) in Columbus, Indiana.  Learn more about the exhibition at the CAMI website (https://camindy.org/exhibitions-all/theblueprint).
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Frances Lightbound: The Land Dissolves in Water | Exhibition
description: Lecture: October 27, 6:30–8pmExhibition: October 27–December 6, 2026, Mon.–Thur. 10am–4pm when IU classes are in session  Lightbound studies the production of space in urban environments, weaving narratives across photography, print, spatial interventions, and sculpture, with a focus on materials and sites in transition.  Architecture becomes an entry-point to questions of land use, ownership and access, bodily experience and perception, and timeframes ranging from the human to the geological. Lightbound invites viewers to consider and participate in the continual (re)construction of meaning in urban environments.  Frances Lightbound holds a B.A. from Glasgow School of Art, Scotland, and an M.F.A. from the School of the Art Institute of Chicago. Recent solo exhibitions include Louise Hopkins Center for the Arts (Lubbock, TX), RULE Gallery (Marfa, TX), and the John David Mooney Foundation (Chicago, IL); her work has been exhibited internationally at venues in London, Glasgow and Berlin. Lightbound is a Lecturer at School of the Art Institute of Chicago in the departments of Print media and Photography.The J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program Lecture and Exhibition Series brings prominent working artists and architects to Columbus. Lectures take place in the auditorium and exhibitions in the gallery, both located within The Republic Building, 333 Second Street in Columbus. The gallery is open Monday through Friday from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. All events are free and open to the public.

title: In Search of Freedom: Stories of Afghanistan Exhibition
description: In Search of Freedom: Stories from Afghanistan  OPEN SEPTEMBER 4, 2026 - DECEMBER 4, 2026, MONDAY - FRIDAY 12-4 PM  OPEN 5-8 PM ON FIRST FRIDAYS OF THE MONTHIn Search of Freedom: Stories from Afghanistancelebrates the beauty, resilience, and rich cultural heritage of Afghanistan through an exhibition of oil paintings by Afghan artist Qahar Behzad, alongside the collaborative mural,August 15: A Mural for Afghanistan.Organized in partnership with Indiana University's Center for Refugee Studies and Exodus Refugee Immigration, the exhibition explores the humanity of the refugee experience through the lens of Afghanistan, inviting visitors to look beyond conflict and discover the stories and experiences of displaced people.The exhibition brings together Qahar's vibrant paintings - which honor Afghanistan's history, traditions, and everyday beauty - withAugust 15: A Mural for Afghanistan,a collaborative project led by Tiffany Black Behzad in collaboration with 59 Afghan evacuees at Camp Atterbury following the fall of Afghanistan to the Taliban on August 15, 2021. Developed through art therapy workshops with Afghan artists Zainab Ahmadi and Fawzia Abdaly, the mural preserves the participants' voices, memories, hopes, and resilience. The mural stands as a record of collective experience and a tribute to those who continue to seek safety, dignity, and freedom against all odds.Together, the artworks present a deeply human portrait of displacement, resilience, and belonging, inviting visitors to reflect on the the universal connections that unite us across borders, traditions, and generations, and the enduring human desire for freedom.
source: Architecture + Design, IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Eskenazi School of Art

Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Momentexamines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers
description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence)  Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. Documents signed by the two other signers—Philip Livingston of New York and James Smith of Pennsylvania—are on display in the North Gallery in The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: Kenny G
description:
Kenny G is the greatest selling instrumental musician of the modern era, and one of the best-selling artists of all time. With global sales totaling more than 75 million records and 1.5 billion streams, the saxophone icon has accumulated a staggering 24-award nominations throughout his 50-year career and has taken home a Grammy Award, American Music Award, two NAACP Awards, Multiple Billboard music awards, and two Soul Train Music Awards. With classic, top-selling studio albums including the best-selling instrumental record of all time with 1992’s 12-times-platinum Breathless, Duotones, Silhouette, Miracles: The Holiday Album, Heart and Soul, and Brazilian Nights, Kenny has maintained a prominent level of creative excellence through decades of unprecedented worldwide commercial success. Kenny G’s music has become part of the global cultural fabric. His song “Going Home” is famously played at the end of each day to signal closing time, across Asia but specifically in China and is immensely popular in Vietnam. At the heart of those achievements is Kenny’s ability to convey deep emotional resonance with his saxophone, a skill never more apparent than on Innocence, his 20th studio album which serves as an homage to heartfelt lullabies, including seven original tracks.
Showing no signs of stopping, Kenny G continues to stretch the boundaries of what instrumental music and musicians can do. Kenny’s longstanding pop culture relevance has transcended the jazz genre. Most recently, he made a cameo in the 2025 Disney+ film, A Very Jonas Christmas Movie, appearing as himself, performing a saxophone solo during “Coming Home This Christmas.” For the last several years, Kenny has taken to the internet with gusto, as new generations of listeners have discovered his music and contemporary hitmakers from nearly  all genres, from The Weeknd to Jon Batiste, have featured him on their tracks, in music videos and even making a surprise appearance at the last MTV Video Music Award’s, opening the show with a live performance with Doja Cat on her single “Jealous Type.” Other notable worldwide campaigns include commercials for Invesco, Google Pixel, Snickers, Audi and a Super Bowl spot for Busch Light’s “Voice of the Mountains,” emphasizing the brand’s “smooth” taste with Kenny playing solo on a mountain top.

title: Eiteljorg Artist In Residence Visiting Lecture: Susan Charlesworth
description:
In celebration of Native Heritage Month, join us for an inspiring afternoon with Susan Charlesworth, an award-winning basket weaver and enrolled citizen of the Choctaw Nation of Oklahoma.
 

Susan is an award-winning basket weaver who first began weaving in 2005, when she entered her baskets into the Choctaw Nation Annual Labor Day Festival and Art Show. Susan has continued to receive awards at multiple Native art markets, including the Eiteljorg Indian Market & Festival. Susan is a retired CNA and social service consultant with a master’s degree in social work and an avid volunteer with the Alzheimer’s Association. She now serves as an Alzheimer’s Association Community Educator in Indianapolis.
 
Event Timeline:• 12:00 PM – 1:00 PM: Lunch served on a first come first serve basis.• 1:00 PM – 2:00 PM: Artist Talk & Presentation by Susan Charlesworth

title: Migrant Remixing: Drag and the Transatlantic Circulation of Andean Latinx Aesthetics
description: As a migrant in the United States, Peruvian soprano Yma Sumac mesmerized mid-twentieth century audiences with her vocal range and her Inca-inspired performance attire. Taking Sumac as a point of departure, this presentation examines the work of contemporary drag performers who similarly draw on Andean cultural imagery as migrant artists in Spain. Vasquez Toral traces a transatlantic circulation of Andean visual culture and Indigeneity through a performance lens that I term "migrant remixing." He focuses on the work of drag performers Gad Yola (Peru) and Inti (Bolivia), examining how their music and drag art are infused with decolonial and anti-racist political urgencies. Collectively, they engage Spain's colonial legacies and the challenges Latinx migrants face in contemporary Spanish society by centering queer Indigenous histories and LGBTQ cultures from the Andes.

title: Daniel Luis Martinez: The Blueprint | Exhibition
location: The Contemporary Art Museum of Indianapolis
description: Opening reception: Friday, October 2, 2026, 6–10pm  Exhibition on view: October 2–December 18, 2026  For this exhibition, the blueprint is used as both a representational and conceptual departure point. Daniel Luis Martinez uses cyanotype printmaking and mixed-media drawing techniques as a generative process to imagine a speculative home on the CAMi campus. The hybrid drawings and prints featured in the exhibition explore the tactile middle-ground of the blueprint as a creative endeavor.  The series employs orthographic conventions typical of architectural drawing sets, though not as precise instructions for building. Rather, a layered and loose approach expresses ideas of home as an architectonic language.  Daniel Luis Martinez is a registered architect, educator, and co-founder of the multi-disciplinary design studio LAA Office, which explores the intersection of landscape, art, and architecture. His research and creative work investigate the potential of public art to generate alternative forms of placemaking. Martinez is Associate Professor and Director of the IU Eskenazi School's J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program (https://architecture.indiana.edu/index.html) in Columbus, Indiana.  Learn more about the exhibition at the CAMI website (https://camindy.org/exhibitions-all/theblueprint).
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Frances Lightbound: The Land Dissolves in Water | Exhibition
description: Lecture: October 27, 6:30–8pmExhibition: October 27–December 6, 2026, Mon.–Thur. 10am–4pm when IU classes are in session  Lightbound studies the production of space in urban environments, weaving narratives across photography, print, spatial interventions, and sculpture, with a focus on materials and sites in transition.  Architecture becomes an entry-point to questions of land use, ownership and access, bodily experience and perception, and timeframes ranging from the human to the geological. Lightbound invites viewers to consider and participate in the continual (re)construction of meaning in urban environments.  Frances Lightbound holds a B.A. from Glasgow School of Art, Scotland, and an M.F.A. from the School of the Art Institute of Chicago. Recent solo exhibitions include Louise Hopkins Center for the Arts (Lubbock, TX), RULE Gallery (Marfa, TX), and the John David Mooney Foundation (Chicago, IL); her work has been exhibited internationally at venues in London, Glasgow and Berlin. Lightbound is a Lecturer at School of the Art Institute of Chicago in the departments of Print media and Photography.The J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program Lecture and Exhibition Series brings prominent working artists and architects to Columbus. Lectures take place in the auditorium and exhibitions in the gallery, both located within The Republic Building, 333 Second Street in Columbus. The gallery is open Monday through Friday from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. All events are free and open to the public.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: In Search of Freedom: Stories of Afghanistan Exhibition
description: In Search of Freedom: Stories from Afghanistan  OPEN SEPTEMBER 4, 2026 - DECEMBER 4, 2026, MONDAY - FRIDAY 12-4 PM  OPEN 5-8 PM ON FIRST FRIDAYS OF THE MONTHIn Search of Freedom: Stories from Afghanistancelebrates the beauty, resilience, and rich cultural heritage of Afghanistan through an exhibition of oil paintings by Afghan artist Qahar Behzad, alongside the collaborative mural,August 15: A Mural for Afghanistan.Organized in partnership with Indiana University's Center for Refugee Studies and Exodus Refugee Immigration, the exhibition explores the humanity of the refugee experience through the lens of Afghanistan, inviting visitors to look beyond conflict and discover the stories and experiences of displaced people.The exhibition brings together Qahar's vibrant paintings - which honor Afghanistan's history, traditions, and everyday beauty - withAugust 15: A Mural for Afghanistan,a collaborative project led by Tiffany Black Behzad in collaboration with 59 Afghan evacuees at Camp Atterbury following the fall of Afghanistan to the Taliban on August 15, 2021. Developed through art therapy workshops with Afghan artists Zainab Ahmadi and Fawzia Abdaly, the mural preserves the participants' voices, memories, hopes, and resilience. The mural stands as a record of collective experience and a tribute to those who continue to seek safety, dignity, and freedom against all odds.Together, the artworks present a deeply human portrait of displacement, resilience, and belonging, inviting visitors to reflect on the the universal connections that unite us across borders, traditions, and generations, and the enduring human desire for freedom.
source: Architecture + Design, IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Eskenazi School of Art

Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Momentexamines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers
description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence)  Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. Documents signed by the two other signers—Philip Livingston of New York and James Smith of Pennsylvania—are on display in the North Gallery in The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: HIV/STI Testing
description: Free HIV Testing & Safer Sex Supplies at the LGBTQ+ Culture Center  Taking care of your sexual health is an important part of your overall well-being, and we're committed to making resources accessible, welcoming, and judgment-free.Positive Link (https://iuhealth.org/find-medical-services/positive-link-hiv-services) provides free and confidential HIV testing in Room 204 of the LGBTQ+ Culture Center every Thursday from 10:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m. during the academic year. During the summer, testing is available on the first and third Thursdays of each month.  In addition, during the academic year, the Monroe County Health Department offers free chlamydia and gonorrhea testing on the third Thursday of every month, also from 10:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m. in Room 101.  The LGBTQ+ Culture Center also offers a variety of free safer sex supplies, including condoms, internal condoms, dental dams, lubricants, and educational materials on proper use. These resources are available to all students, free of charge. You can find them in the kitchenette area near the back entrance of the Center and are welcome to take what you need.  STI Testing & Safer Sex Resources Beyond Campus  Prioritizing your sexual health should be simple and accessible. In addition to services available at the LGBTQ+ Culture Center, students can receive testing on campus through the IU Student Health Center (https://healthcenter.indiana.edu/medical/sti-testing/index.html) or visit several local organizations (https://healthcenter.indiana.edu/health-answers/sexual-health/sti-testing-resources.html) that offer free or low-cost testing and prevention services.  Many of these providers offer confidential care, safer sex supplies, and supportive information about prevention, treatment, and sexual wellness. If you're unsure where to start, we're happy to help connect you with resources that fit your needs.All Indiana University events, groups, activities, educational, cultural, and historical observances welcome all members of the Indiana University community.

description: Outfitting IU Athletics: Hoosier Champions                  This exhibit showcases objects from IU's championship teams and athletes, connecting them to historic achievements in the Big Ten and the national stage. title: Indiana Tax Court Oral Argument
location: LOWELL E. BAIER HALL/IU MAURER SCHOOL OF LAW
description: The Indiana Tax Court will visit the IU Maurer School of Law to hear oral argument in Northern Indiana Public Service Company, LLC v. Indiana Department of State Revenue, Case No. 24T-TA-00017.   The Tax Court is a specialized appellate court with exclusive jurisdiction over appeals from final determinations of the Indiana Department of State Revenue and the Indiana Board of Tax Review and certain appeals from the Department of Local Government Finance. It hears disputes over state and local taxes, including property, income, sales, and excise taxes, which touch the finances of Hoosier individuals, families, and businesses alike.  Attendees will have a rare chance to see this specialized court in action. Because the Tax Court's decisions are reviewed directly by the Indiana Supreme Court, rather than by the Court of Appeals, the proceedings offer a distinctive look at how Indiana's tax system is shaped by the judiciary.  A summary of the case can be found here (https://events.iu.edu/live/files/8523-nipsco-bench-memopdf). Following the argument, attendees may participate in an informal Q&A session with the judge and attorneys. While food is not permitted during the argument, food is allowed during the Q&A.  Attendees are asked to observe courtroom etiquette:Remove hats before entering the courtroom.  Stand when judges enter and leave the courtroom.  Turn off or silence cell phones before entering the courtroom. Do not use phones while court is in session.  No video, audio recording, or photography is allowed once court is in session.  No food or beverages are allowed in the courtroom  Refrain from speaking during the proceedings

title: The Paradox of Precommitment: Making Constitutions in Deeply Divided Societies
description: How can constitutions provide stability when the most contested political questions remain unresolved? Using Ethiopia's 1995 Constitution as a case study, this talk explores the paradox of constitutional precommitment and the risks of entrenching disputed issues such as sovereignty, self-determination, and territorial authority. Drawing on constitutional theory, history, and institutional analysis, it argues that durable constitutional systems require both strong protections for democratic governance and credible mechanisms for revisiting unsettled foundational questions.  About the speaker: Alemayehu Fentaw Weldemariam is a CCD PhD Fellow at the IU Maurer School of Law.

title: Scholarly Write-In
description:
Write and work in solidarity with other IU scholars. We offer a silent work environment with coffee and natural light. The write-in is open to all graduate students (at any stage of their degree program).

We will check in at the beginning of our meeting, set some goals together, then work independently for a few hours. Fifteen minutes prior to the close of the meeting, we will reconvene to update each other on our progress and set broad goals for the coming week.

This is a casual meeting – feel free to come for as much or as little time as you like, and only during the weeks that work for you. You are welcome and encouraged to work on anything that you need time and space for: participants regularly work on dissertations, course papers, syllabi and lesson plans, articles and pieces for publication, and grading. Our goal is to create a space where we can work together in solidarity on whatever projects we need to each week.

Meets weekly throughout the semester, Thursdays from 1-4pm. No meeting during Thanksgiving break.

Co-sponsored by Writing Tutorial Services and the IU Libraries.

title: Concentus – Dana Marsh, director
description: Repertoire to be announcedAbout the DirectorDana Marsh is professor of music (early music/voice), chair of Historical Performance, and director of the Historical Performance Institute at the Indiana University Jacobs School of Music. He coaches singers in historical performance and teaches courses in early notation, performance practice, and musical rhetoric, and has directed Jacobs ensemble recordings for national broadcast on NPR. Beyond IU, Marsh is artistic director of the Washington Bach Consort, where since 2018, he has shaped the ensemble's artistic vision through multi‑year projects and major choral‑orchestral repertoire. The Washington Post has written that under his leadership, the Consort "could go head‑to‑head with period‑performance ensembles anywhere." Marsh focuses on how text, rhetoric, and musical gesture animate historical repertories in performance. As a guest conductor, Marsh has collaborated with leading ensembles in the United States and abroad, including the Choirs and Baroque Orchestra of Washington National Cathedral, Trinity Baroque Orchestra and the Choir of Trinity Wall Street, Cappella Romana, Bach Collegium San Diego, Portland Baroque Orchestra, London Mozart Players, and Studio de musique ancienne de Montréal, as well as at the Lamèque International Baroque Festival. Trained as a chorister at St. Thomas Choir School in New York and Salisbury Cathedral, Marsh earned his undergraduate degree in organ performance from the Eastman School of Music and completed master's and doctoral degrees in historical musicology at the University of Oxford. Before focusing primarily on conducting, he enjoyed an international career as a countertenor and consort singer (1992-2008). He was a core member of the Choir of New College, Oxford, recording extensively and touring internationally; one recording received a Gramophone Early Music Award. As a singer, he appeared with ensembles including the Academy of Ancient Music, American Bach Soloists, Musica Angelica, Seattle Baroque Orchestra, and the New York Collegium under Gustav Leonhardt.

title: Daniel Luis Martinez: The Blueprint | Exhibition
location: The Contemporary Art Museum of Indianapolis
description: Opening reception: Friday, October 2, 2026, 6–10pm  Exhibition on view: October 2–December 18, 2026  For this exhibition, the blueprint is used as both a representational and conceptual departure point. Daniel Luis Martinez uses cyanotype printmaking and mixed-media drawing techniques as a generative process to imagine a speculative home on the CAMi campus. The hybrid drawings and prints featured in the exhibition explore the tactile middle-ground of the blueprint as a creative endeavor.  The series employs orthographic conventions typical of architectural drawing sets, though not as precise instructions for building. Rather, a layered and loose approach expresses ideas of home as an architectonic language.  Daniel Luis Martinez is a registered architect, educator, and co-founder of the multi-disciplinary design studio LAA Office, which explores the intersection of landscape, art, and architecture. His research and creative work investigate the potential of public art to generate alternative forms of placemaking. Martinez is Associate Professor and Director of the IU Eskenazi School's J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program (https://architecture.indiana.edu/index.html) in Columbus, Indiana.  Learn more about the exhibition at the CAMI website (https://camindy.org/exhibitions-all/theblueprint).
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Frances Lightbound: The Land Dissolves in Water | Exhibition
description: Lecture: October 27, 6:30–8pmExhibition: October 27–December 6, 2026, Mon.–Thur. 10am–4pm when IU classes are in session  Lightbound studies the production of space in urban environments, weaving narratives across photography, print, spatial interventions, and sculpture, with a focus on materials and sites in transition.  Architecture becomes an entry-point to questions of land use, ownership and access, bodily experience and perception, and timeframes ranging from the human to the geological. Lightbound invites viewers to consider and participate in the continual (re)construction of meaning in urban environments.  Frances Lightbound holds a B.A. from Glasgow School of Art, Scotland, and an M.F.A. from the School of the Art Institute of Chicago. Recent solo exhibitions include Louise Hopkins Center for the Arts (Lubbock, TX), RULE Gallery (Marfa, TX), and the John David Mooney Foundation (Chicago, IL); her work has been exhibited internationally at venues in London, Glasgow and Berlin. Lightbound is a Lecturer at School of the Art Institute of Chicago in the departments of Print media and Photography.The J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program Lecture and Exhibition Series brings prominent working artists and architects to Columbus. Lectures take place in the auditorium and exhibitions in the gallery, both located within The Republic Building, 333 Second Street in Columbus. The gallery is open Monday through Friday from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. All events are free and open to the public.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: In Search of Freedom: Stories of Afghanistan Exhibition
description: In Search of Freedom: Stories from Afghanistan  OPEN SEPTEMBER 4, 2026 - DECEMBER 4, 2026, MONDAY - FRIDAY 12-4 PM  OPEN 5-8 PM ON FIRST FRIDAYS OF THE MONTHIn Search of Freedom: Stories from Afghanistancelebrates the beauty, resilience, and rich cultural heritage of Afghanistan through an exhibition of oil paintings by Afghan artist Qahar Behzad, alongside the collaborative mural,August 15: A Mural for Afghanistan.Organized in partnership with Indiana University's Center for Refugee Studies and Exodus Refugee Immigration, the exhibition explores the humanity of the refugee experience through the lens of Afghanistan, inviting visitors to look beyond conflict and discover the stories and experiences of displaced people.The exhibition brings together Qahar's vibrant paintings - which honor Afghanistan's history, traditions, and everyday beauty - withAugust 15: A Mural for Afghanistan,a collaborative project led by Tiffany Black Behzad in collaboration with 59 Afghan evacuees at Camp Atterbury following the fall of Afghanistan to the Taliban on August 15, 2021. Developed through art therapy workshops with Afghan artists Zainab Ahmadi and Fawzia Abdaly, the mural preserves the participants' voices, memories, hopes, and resilience. The mural stands as a record of collective experience and a tribute to those who continue to seek safety, dignity, and freedom against all odds.Together, the artworks present a deeply human portrait of displacement, resilience, and belonging, inviting visitors to reflect on the the universal connections that unite us across borders, traditions, and generations, and the enduring human desire for freedom.
source: Architecture + Design, IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Eskenazi School of Art

Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Momentexamines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers
description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence)  Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. Documents signed by the two other signers—Philip Livingston of New York and James Smith of Pennsylvania—are on display in the North Gallery in The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

description: Going to college offers a variety of new freedoms, excitements, and difficulties as students make the transition away from home. title: IJGLS Symposium
location: LOWELL E. BAIER HALL/IU MAURER SCHOOL OF LAW
description: Climate change, pollution, and biodiversity loss are intensifying worldwide, and their heaviest burdens fall on the world's most vulnerable populations and indigenous communities. An estimated 1.5 billion people lack basic access to redress for environmental harms through political, administrative, or legal channels. Many of these communities also lack skilled advocates, and the lawyers and nonlawyers who do take up their causes face growing harassment and physical attacks.  The Indiana Journal of Global Legal Studies has brought together scholars from across the Americas to examine where marginalized communities, their advocates, and the governance systems that too often leave them behind intersect.For a full list of panels and presenters, view the full schedule here (https://events.iu.edu/live/files/8597-ijgls-symposium-fall-2026-schedulepdf).   Papers presented at the symposium will be published in Volume 34 Issue 2 of the Journal.

When that organization closed, they donated their materials to IU. Steele, Indiana University's First Artist in ResidenceCapturing the Campus pays tribute to renowned Hoosier artist T.C. Steele. The exhibit honors the century that has passed since his death by showcasing paintings form the artist's residency at IU and other relevant works. The exhibit will bring together Steele's landscapes from the IU Public Art and Cultural Heritage Collection and the Indiana State Museum and Historic Sites' collection, allowing the holdings of these two collections to be viewed in one space. location: Fine Arts Building, 1201 East 7th Street, Bloomington, IN 47405
description: In this talk, Kristýna Milde shares their 15-year investigation into how trees, forests, newspapers, architecture, urban infrastructure, and living materials can become sites for questioning the boundaries between nature and culture and the search for connection.   The Czech-American interdisciplinary artist duo based in Brooklyn, New York works across sculpture, site-specific installation, photography, and animation, combining living plants, transformed materials, and everyday objects to create evolving environments that reveal the interconnectedness of forests, cities, and the cultural spaces we inhabit.  Recipients of the 2026 NYSCA/NYFA Artist Fellowship in Sculpture, their work has been featured in The New York Times, The Brooklyn Rail, Flash Art, Hyperallergic, Forbes, and Czech television and radio, among others. The College of Arts and Sciences and the Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design gratefully acknowledge Dr. Meredith McKinney (B.A. '65) and Elsa Luise Barthel McKinney (B.A. '65) for their love of the arts and their generous support in endowing the McKinney Visiting Artist Series at Indiana University Bloomington.

title: Daniel Luis Martinez: The Blueprint | Exhibition
location: The Contemporary Art Museum of Indianapolis
description: Opening reception: Friday, October 2, 2026, 6–10pm  Exhibition on view: October 2–December 18, 2026  For this exhibition, the blueprint is used as both a representational and conceptual departure point. Daniel Luis Martinez uses cyanotype printmaking and mixed-media drawing techniques as a generative process to imagine a speculative home on the CAMi campus. The hybrid drawings and prints featured in the exhibition explore the tactile middle-ground of the blueprint as a creative endeavor.  The series employs orthographic conventions typical of architectural drawing sets, though not as precise instructions for building. Rather, a layered and loose approach expresses ideas of home as an architectonic language.  Daniel Luis Martinez is a registered architect, educator, and co-founder of the multi-disciplinary design studio LAA Office, which explores the intersection of landscape, art, and architecture. His research and creative work investigate the potential of public art to generate alternative forms of placemaking. Martinez is Associate Professor and Director of the IU Eskenazi School's J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program (https://architecture.indiana.edu/index.html) in Columbus, Indiana.  Learn more about the exhibition at the CAMI website (https://camindy.org/exhibitions-all/theblueprint).
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Frances Lightbound: The Land Dissolves in Water | Exhibition
description: Lecture: October 27, 6:30–8pmExhibition: October 27–December 6, 2026, Mon.–Thur. 10am–4pm when IU classes are in session  Lightbound studies the production of space in urban environments, weaving narratives across photography, print, spatial interventions, and sculpture, with a focus on materials and sites in transition.  Architecture becomes an entry-point to questions of land use, ownership and access, bodily experience and perception, and timeframes ranging from the human to the geological. Lightbound invites viewers to consider and participate in the continual (re)construction of meaning in urban environments.  Frances Lightbound holds a B.A. from Glasgow School of Art, Scotland, and an M.F.A. from the School of the Art Institute of Chicago. Recent solo exhibitions include Louise Hopkins Center for the Arts (Lubbock, TX), RULE Gallery (Marfa, TX), and the John David Mooney Foundation (Chicago, IL); her work has been exhibited internationally at venues in London, Glasgow and Berlin. Lightbound is a Lecturer at School of the Art Institute of Chicago in the departments of Print media and Photography.The J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program Lecture and Exhibition Series brings prominent working artists and architects to Columbus. Lectures take place in the auditorium and exhibitions in the gallery, both located within The Republic Building, 333 Second Street in Columbus. The gallery is open Monday through Friday from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. All events are free and open to the public.

title: In Search of Freedom: Stories of Afghanistan Exhibition
description: In Search of Freedom: Stories from Afghanistan  OPEN SEPTEMBER 4, 2026 - DECEMBER 4, 2026, MONDAY - FRIDAY 12-4 PM  OPEN 5-8 PM ON FIRST FRIDAYS OF THE MONTHIn Search of Freedom: Stories from Afghanistancelebrates the beauty, resilience, and rich cultural heritage of Afghanistan through an exhibition of oil paintings by Afghan artist Qahar Behzad, alongside the collaborative mural,August 15: A Mural for Afghanistan.Organized in partnership with Indiana University's Center for Refugee Studies and Exodus Refugee Immigration, the exhibition explores the humanity of the refugee experience through the lens of Afghanistan, inviting visitors to look beyond conflict and discover the stories and experiences of displaced people.The exhibition brings together Qahar's vibrant paintings - which honor Afghanistan's history, traditions, and everyday beauty - withAugust 15: A Mural for Afghanistan,a collaborative project led by Tiffany Black Behzad in collaboration with 59 Afghan evacuees at Camp Atterbury following the fall of Afghanistan to the Taliban on August 15, 2021. Developed through art therapy workshops with Afghan artists Zainab Ahmadi and Fawzia Abdaly, the mural preserves the participants' voices, memories, hopes, and resilience. The mural stands as a record of collective experience and a tribute to those who continue to seek safety, dignity, and freedom against all odds.Together, the artworks present a deeply human portrait of displacement, resilience, and belonging, inviting visitors to reflect on the the universal connections that unite us across borders, traditions, and generations, and the enduring human desire for freedom.
source: Architecture + Design, IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Eskenazi School of Art

Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Momentexamines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers
description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence)  Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. Documents signed by the two other signers—Philip Livingston of New York and James Smith of Pennsylvania—are on display in the North Gallery in The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: Hidden Mythologies: Karelian Traditions & Myths
location: IU Museum of Archaeology and Anthropology, 416 N. Indiana Ave., Bloomington, IN 47408
description: Event Details:  Now in its second year, the Hidden Mythologieslecture series explores the rich and often overlooked mythological traditions of the peoples of the Volga-Ural region and beyond. Through stories of gods, spirits, legendary heroes, sacred landscapes, and traditional beliefs, the series examines the ways mythology reflects and preserves the cultures and worldviews of diverse communities across Eurasia.  Journey into the forests and mythological traditions of the Karelian people, exploring the Meteliläinens and the celebrated Finnish-Karelian epic, the Kalevala. Discover a world in which the forest, poetry, magic, and mythology are deeply intertwined. The program features traditional Karelian ballads, including Vellamon Neidon Onginta, Kanteleen Synty, and Loitsu Saunassa. The program concludes with a live performance of the Karelia folk song Kukkuu - Kukkuu.  Each program begins with a presentation by Dr. Golshat Safiullina exploring an aspect of the featured culture's mythological traditions, followed by Folk Song Club, an interactive musical experience curated by musical director Daryana Antipova, bringing another dimension to the stories, beliefs, and cultural heritage explored in the lecture.  This event is held in collaboration with the Slavic and East European Languages Department, the Jacobs School of Music, and the CHAKCHAK: Languages and Cultures Foundation.Parking Information:  Limited complimentary parking is available in front of the Museum entrance (https://maps.app.goo.gl/k4Txsojst2gSW5fUA) off Indiana Avenue. Free street parking is available in surrounding neighborhoods on weekends and weekdays after 5:00 PM.  Paid parking is also available in the University Collections at McCalla (https://maps.app.goo.gl/3i62KNcjDeCACruHA) parking lot off Indiana Avenue and the Indiana Memorial Union (https://maps.app.goo.gl/2n49VoLuF78o5twJA) visitor lot.  Metered street parking is available near Sample Gates and throughout downtown Bloomington, including along Kirkwood Avenue, East 6th Street, East 4th Street, North Lincoln Street, North Dunn Street, and South Grant Street.Questions?  For accessibility assistance or questions about this event, please reach out to Camden Hill at camrhill@iu.edu (mailto:camrhill@iu.edu) or (812) 855-1696.Note:  By attending this event, you agree to be in photography that may be used by the University for promotional purposes. If you would not like to be in any pictures, please speak to a Museum staff member and they will inform assigned photographers of your request. If you see that your image has been used in error, please reach out to iumaa@iu.edu (mailto:iumaa@iu.edu) to request that it be taken down.

title: Daniel Luis Martinez: The Blueprint | Exhibition
location: The Contemporary Art Museum of Indianapolis
description: Opening reception: Friday, October 2, 2026, 6–10pm  Exhibition on view: October 2–December 18, 2026  For this exhibition, the blueprint is used as both a representational and conceptual departure point. Daniel Luis Martinez uses cyanotype printmaking and mixed-media drawing techniques as a generative process to imagine a speculative home on the CAMi campus. The hybrid drawings and prints featured in the exhibition explore the tactile middle-ground of the blueprint as a creative endeavor.  The series employs orthographic conventions typical of architectural drawing sets, though not as precise instructions for building. Rather, a layered and loose approach expresses ideas of home as an architectonic language.  Daniel Luis Martinez is a registered architect, educator, and co-founder of the multi-disciplinary design studio LAA Office, which explores the intersection of landscape, art, and architecture. His research and creative work investigate the potential of public art to generate alternative forms of placemaking. Martinez is Associate Professor and Director of the IU Eskenazi School's J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program (https://architecture.indiana.edu/index.html) in Columbus, Indiana.  Learn more about the exhibition at the CAMI website (https://camindy.org/exhibitions-all/theblueprint).
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Frances Lightbound: The Land Dissolves in Water | Exhibition
description: Lecture: October 27, 6:30–8pmExhibition: October 27–December 6, 2026, Mon.–Thur. 10am–4pm when IU classes are in session  Lightbound studies the production of space in urban environments, weaving narratives across photography, print, spatial interventions, and sculpture, with a focus on materials and sites in transition.  Architecture becomes an entry-point to questions of land use, ownership and access, bodily experience and perception, and timeframes ranging from the human to the geological. Lightbound invites viewers to consider and participate in the continual (re)construction of meaning in urban environments.  Frances Lightbound holds a B.A. from Glasgow School of Art, Scotland, and an M.F.A. from the School of the Art Institute of Chicago. Recent solo exhibitions include Louise Hopkins Center for the Arts (Lubbock, TX), RULE Gallery (Marfa, TX), and the John David Mooney Foundation (Chicago, IL); her work has been exhibited internationally at venues in London, Glasgow and Berlin. Lightbound is a Lecturer at School of the Art Institute of Chicago in the departments of Print media and Photography.The J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program Lecture and Exhibition Series brings prominent working artists and architects to Columbus. Lectures take place in the auditorium and exhibitions in the gallery, both located within The Republic Building, 333 Second Street in Columbus. The gallery is open Monday through Friday from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. All events are free and open to the public.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: In Search of Freedom: Stories of Afghanistan Exhibition
description: In Search of Freedom: Stories from Afghanistan  OPEN SEPTEMBER 4, 2026 - DECEMBER 4, 2026, MONDAY - FRIDAY 12-4 PM  OPEN 5-8 PM ON FIRST FRIDAYS OF THE MONTHIn Search of Freedom: Stories from Afghanistancelebrates the beauty, resilience, and rich cultural heritage of Afghanistan through an exhibition of oil paintings by Afghan artist Qahar Behzad, alongside the collaborative mural,August 15: A Mural for Afghanistan.Organized in partnership with Indiana University's Center for Refugee Studies and Exodus Refugee Immigration, the exhibition explores the humanity of the refugee experience through the lens of Afghanistan, inviting visitors to look beyond conflict and discover the stories and experiences of displaced people.The exhibition brings together Qahar's vibrant paintings - which honor Afghanistan's history, traditions, and everyday beauty - withAugust 15: A Mural for Afghanistan,a collaborative project led by Tiffany Black Behzad in collaboration with 59 Afghan evacuees at Camp Atterbury following the fall of Afghanistan to the Taliban on August 15, 2021. Developed through art therapy workshops with Afghan artists Zainab Ahmadi and Fawzia Abdaly, the mural preserves the participants' voices, memories, hopes, and resilience. The mural stands as a record of collective experience and a tribute to those who continue to seek safety, dignity, and freedom against all odds.Together, the artworks present a deeply human portrait of displacement, resilience, and belonging, inviting visitors to reflect on the the universal connections that unite us across borders, traditions, and generations, and the enduring human desire for freedom.

title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Momentexamines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers
description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence)  Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. Documents signed by the two other signers—Philip Livingston of New York and James Smith of Pennsylvania—are on display in the North Gallery in The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: Home Away from Home: Student Life on Campus
description: Going to college offers a variety of new freedoms, excitements, and difficulties as students make the transition away from home.  Spanning across four decades—1970s to the 2000s—items including scrapbooks, photographs, student papers, and handbooks demonstrate life on and off campus. From decorating dorm rooms to chasing campus ghosts, students have always found ways to build community and make new memories. This exhibit highlights the student experience and the multitude of ways students found a sense of home, identity and belonging at Indiana University.
